entries.title: WABISABI
entries.body: Central-coordinator coinjoin protocol used on the Wasabi 2.0 wallet. This model was designed by Ádám Ficsór (nopara73), Yuval Kogman, Lucas Ontivero and István András Seres in 2021, and was integrated into the Wasabi 2.0 software the following year.

entries.title: WALLET OF SATOSHI
entries.body:
Mobile wallet specialized in payments via the Lightning Network. Wallet of Satoshi is designed to offer a simplified user experience: the user can send and receive Lightning payments in a few seconds, without any technical configuration.

Historically, Wallet of Satoshi operated on a *custodial* model: the company held the private keys and managed the funds on behalf of the user. This model simplifies use, but involves a trade-off: the user must trust the provider with the custody of their bitcoins. Since 2025, WoS also offers, as an option, an integration of the Spark protocol, thereby making it possible to adopt a *self-custodial* model.

entries.title: WALLET.DAT
entries.body: File in Bitcoin Core that stores information about the user's wallet, such as private keys and completed transactions. The `wallet.dat` file can be encrypted by the user to secure the funds, but it is not encrypted by default. Since version 0.16.0, this file has been moved to the `/wallets` folder.

entries.title: WALLETS/DB.LOG
entries.body: Log file in Bitcoin Core specific to the wallet database. It records the operations and events related to the wallet database for troubleshooting.

entries.title: WASABI WALLET
entries.body: Privacy-focused Bitcoin wallet offering features such as coinjoin.

entries.title: WATCH-ONLY WALLET
entries.body: A watch-only wallet is a type of software that allows a user to view the transactions associated with a specific Bitcoin key or set of keys, without owning the corresponding private keys. It provides visibility into the balance and transaction history, without however allowing the wallet's funds to be spent. For example, the Sentinel application is a watch-only wallet.

entries.title: WATCHMEN
entries.body: In the context of Liquid (a Bitcoin sidechain), these are entities responsible for maintaining the peg of L-BTC, Liquid's native token, by managing and securing the underlying BTC. They ensure that the assets transferred between the main Bitcoin blockchain and the Liquid sidechain are correctly locked and unlocked. The goal of their actions is to maintain the same value between the L-BTC circulating on Liquid and the BTC circulating on Bitcoin. In Liquid, the watchmen are among the functionaries, alongside the *blocksigners*.

entries.title: WATCHTOWER
entries.body:
External service that monitors the Bitcoin blockchain in place of a Lightning node to detect any attempt to cheat on its channels. If a dishonest peer publishes an old commitment transaction while the node is offline, the watchtower automatically broadcasts the corresponding justice transaction to recover all of the channel's funds before the *timelock* expires.

The mechanism is designed to preserve the node's privacy: with each update of a channel, the node encrypts the pre-signed penalty transaction with the TXID of the relevant commitment transaction, then sends the watchtower this encrypted blob along with a truncated portion of the TXID. The watchtower can only decrypt the transaction if it observes a matching TXID on the blockchain by means of the truncated portion, that is, in the event of actual cheating. It therefore has no visibility into the identity of peers, the balances or the structure of the channels during normal operation. It will learn this information only in the event of cheating.

The watchtower constitutes a minimal trusted third party: it can neither modify nor divert the funds, since the justice transaction is already signed with outputs fixed in favor of the channel's owner. The only risk for the node is to rely on a watchtower that would not fulfill its role at the moment it is actually needed. This is why a node can configure several of them, in order to ensure that at least one of them will act correctly when needed.

There are so-called "altruistic" watchtowers, which are offered publicly and free of charge, and any Lightning node can also play this role for other nodes.

entries.title: WEIGHT UNIT - WU
entries.body:
Unit of measurement introduced by SegWit (BIP-0141) to quantify the space that a transaction or a block occupies relative to the maximum authorized limit. Each *weight unit* (WU) represents 1/4,000,000th of the maximum capacity of a block. This unit replaces the raw byte measurement that was used before SegWit, and makes it possible to apply a differentiated weighting depending on the nature of the data in a transaction.

The calculation of a transaction's weight rests on a distinction between *non-witness* data (version, inputs, outputs, *locktime*) and *witness* data (signatures, public keys and other proof elements added by SegWit). The formula is as follows:
```math
poids\ =\ taille\ sans\ witness \times 4\ +\ taille\ du\ witness \times 1
```
In other words, each byte of *non-witness* data counts for 4 WU, whereas each byte of *witness* data counts for only 1 WU. For a *legacy* transaction (without SegWit), there is no *witness* data, so the weight is simply 4 times the size in bytes. For example, a standard *legacy* P2PKH transaction of 226 bytes weighs `226 \times 4 = 904` WU.

For an equivalent SegWit transaction (P2WPKH, 1 input, 2 outputs), the total size is approximately 222 bytes, including approximately 110 bytes of *witness* (signature and public key). The weight is then:
```math
112 \times 4 + 110 \times 1 = 448 + 110 = 558\ WU
```
This represents a reduction of approximately 38% compared to the equivalent *legacy* transaction, which makes it possible to include more transactions in a block.

The block limit is set at 4,000,000 WU. If a block contains only *legacy* transactions, this limit is equivalent to the former limit of 1,000,000 bytes (`1\,000\,000 \times 4 = 4\,000\,000`), which ensures backward compatibility with nodes that have not been updated. In practice, with a majority of SegWit transactions, blocks reach approximately 2 to 3 MB in actual size. The theoretical maximum approaches 4 MB, but only in the pathological case of a block filled almost exclusively with *witness* data.

To convert a weight into virtual bytes (*vbytes*), simply divide by 4: `vbytes\ =\ poids\ /\ 4`. Transaction fees are generally expressed in sat/vB (satoshis per *vbyte*).

entries.title: WHALE
entries.body: Refers to an individual or entity that owns a very large quantity of bitcoins.

entries.title: WHIRLPOOL
entries.body: ZeroLink Chaumian coinjoin protocol, developed by the Samourai Wallet team. Whirlpool was available on the Samourai Wallet (Android), Sparrow Wallet (PC) and Bitcoin Keeper (iOS and Android) wallets.

entries.title: WHIRLPOOL STAT TOOL
entries.body: Command-line software developed by Samourai Wallet that provides the prospective and retrospective anonsets of a mixed coin within Whirlpool, as well as its diffusion rate in the pool. WST uses the HyperLogLogPlusPlus algorithm, which makes it possible to estimate the number of distinct values in a very large data set.

entries.title: WHITE PAPER
entries.body:
Report or guide that informs readers concisely about a complex issue. In the case of Bitcoin, it is the name given to the scientific document titled "*Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System*" published by Satoshi Nakamoto for the first time on October 31, 2008. This document describes the fundamental principles of Bitcoin. The White Paper presented nowadays is a second version published on March 24, 2009.

*To download the Bitcoin White Paper: https://bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf.*

entries.title: WIF - WALLET IMPORT FORMAT
entries.body: Method for encoding a Bitcoin private key so that it can be imported or exported more easily between different wallets. WIF is built on a `Base58Check` encoding, which includes information about the version, the compression of the corresponding public key and a checksum for detecting input errors. A WIF private key begins with the characters `5` for uncompressed keys, or `K` and `L` for compressed keys, and contains all the characters needed to reconstruct the original private key. The WIF format provides a standardized way to transfer a private key between different wallet software.

entries.title: WITNESS TRANSACTION
entries.body: In the context of the RGB protocol, the Witness Transaction designates the Bitcoin transaction that closes the Single-use Seal around a message incorporating a Multi Protocol Commitment (MPC). This operation consists of spending an existing UTXO, thereby closing the previous seal, while creating a new output containing a commitment to a new seal definition, in order to lock in the contractual commitment recorded in the protocol. The Witness Transaction thus constitutes on-chain proof that the state of the RGB contract was fixed at a specific moment.

entries.title: WITNESSSCRIPT
entries.body:
Script that specifies the conditions under which bitcoins can be spent in P2WSH or P2SH-P2WSH UTXOs. Typically, the `witnessScript` determine the conditions of a multisig wallet under the SegWit standard. In these script standards, the `scriptPubKey` of the UTXO (the output) contains a hash of the `witnessScript`. To use this UTXO as an input in a new transaction, the holder must reveal the original `witnessScript`, in order to prove its match with the digest in the `scriptPubKey`. The `witnessScript` must then be included in the `scriptWitness` of the transaction, which also contains the elements needed to validate the script, such as signatures.  The `witnessScript` is thus the SegWit equivalent of the `redeemScript` in a P2SH transaction, with the difference that it is placed in the transaction's witness, and not in the `scriptSig`.

*Note, the `witnessScript` must not be confused with the `scriptWitness`. While the `witnessScript` defines the spending conditions of a P2WSH or P2SH-P2WSH UTXO and is a script in its own right, the `scriptWitness` contains the witness data of any SegWit input.*

entries.title: WIZARDSARDINE
entries.body:
Company specialized in the security and custody of bitcoins, founded in 2020 by Kevin Loaec and Antoine Poinsot, and incorporated in the Azores (Portugal). Wizardsardine develops open source Bitcoin wallet management solutions, with an emphasis on advanced security mechanisms such as *vaults* and configurable spending policies.

The company is behind the Revault protocol, an institutional custody system using pre-signed transactions and *watchtowers* to secure organizations' funds. Wizardsardine also develops Liana, a Bitcoin wallet that leverages Miniscript to offer recovery and inheritance configurations based on *timelocks*.

entries.title: WRENCH ATTACK
frenchAliases: ATTAQUE À LA CLÉ À MOLETTE
entries.body:
Physical attack that aims to force a bitcoin holder to hand over their funds under threat or through violence. The name refers to a cheap wrench (with a symbolic value of 5 dollars) used as a tool of coercion, and illustrates the idea that the most robust cryptography can be bypassed by a simple physical assault.

Several countermeasures exist to limit the risks related to this attack. The use of a BIP-0039 passphrase makes it possible to create a hidden wallet, which offers a form of plausible deniability. The use of multisig with a geographic distribution of keys prevents an attacker from obtaining all the necessary signatures in a single place. Timelocks can also be employed to make funds temporarily inaccessible. Finally, discretion about one's bitcoin holdings remains the most basic preventive measure.

This notion is a reminder that security in the Bitcoin ecosystem is a global issue that goes beyond the computing dimension alone. It also involves operational security (OPSEC) considerations and physical protection.

entries.title: WTXID
entries.body: Extension of the traditional TXID, including the witness data (*witness*) introduced with SegWit. Whereas the TXID is a hash of the transaction data excluding the witness, the WTXID is the `SHA256d` of the entirety of the transaction data, witness included. WTXIDs are stored in a second Merkle tree whose root is placed in the coinbase transaction. This separation makes it possible to eliminate the malleability of the transaction's TXID.

entries.title: WUMBO CHANNEL
entries.body:
High-capacity Lightning channel, exceeding the historical limit of 16,777,215 satoshis (approximately 0.168 BTC) imposed by default on the first nodes. This limit, encoded on 24 bits, had been introduced as a precaution during the early years of the Lightning Network to limit potential losses in the event of a bug in the implementations.

Subsequently, implementations introduced an option allowing channels of up to 10 BTC to be accepted. These high-capacity channels are nicknamed "Wumbo channels", in reference to an episode of *SpongeBob SquarePants*.
